name: Avotermin (Juvista)

card.summary: An investigational recombinant TGF-beta3 injected into wound edges at surgery, developed to make healed scars look less visible.
card.note: Never marketed; phase III results reported in 2011 did not meet endpoints.

quick.overview:
Avotermin is a recombinant version of transforming growth factor beta 3, a protein linked to scar-free healing in embryonic skin. It was developed under the brand name Juvista to be given by injection into the edges of a surgical wound, with the aim of leaving a flatter, less noticeable scar.

Early randomized trials in volunteers and patients reported improved scar appearance, but a later phase III program failed to meet its endpoints and the drug was not approved.
quick.how: In trials it was injected into the skin around a wound at the time of surgery, by clinicians, within placebo-controlled studies. It is not available as a marketed product.
quick.risks: In trials it was reported as having an acceptable safety profile in the studies published. Because TGF-beta isoforms are linked to tumour biology, reviews examined whether TGF-beta3 could affect cancer risk and concluded the evidence points to no causal role, though functional data are limited. It is not approved anywhere.

lead: Avotermin (planned brand name Juvista) is recombinant human transforming growth factor beta 3 (TGF-beta3), developed to improve the appearance of scars. Because scars from surgery or injury are a visible cosmetic concern, it was designed as a preventive treatment given around the time of wounding rather than a treatment for old scars [1][3].

The rationale came from research showing that embryonic wounds heal without scarring and that TGF-beta3 regulates that scar-free pattern. Adding it to adult wounds in animal models reduced early matrix deposition and produced tissue organized more like normal skin [3]. Reviews describe it as the first of a new class of prophylactic scar medicines [1][5][6].

Phase I/II studies published in The Lancet in 2009 and several phase II trials reported scar improvement [10][7][8][9]. A phase III program then failed in 2011; the developer's shares were reported to have fallen about 75% [12]. It has never been marketed.

chain: Injected into wound edges at surgery
angle.text: In trials, avotermin was injected into the margins of fresh incisions so the scar would look less visible as it matured. It is investigational and available only in research settings, if at all.

infobox: Investigational; phase III did not meet endpoints (2011)

paras: Avotermin was studied for prophylactic scar reduction after surgical incisions, scar revision surgery, skin graft donor sites, breast surgery and varicose vein removal [8][9][10]. Authors noted that physicians and patients value even small improvements in scar appearance and that no pharmaceutical for prophylactic scar reduction was marketed [1][6].

TGF-beta3 is a cytokine tied to the scar-free healing seen in embryos. In adult animal wounds it reduced early extracellular matrix deposition and the matrix formed with an architecture closer to normal skin [3].

Three double-blind, placebo-controlled phase I/II studies in The Lancet in 2009 examined prophylactic avotermin for scarring [10]. A phase II trial published in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery in 2010 tested administration into wound margins of incisions [9]. In 2011 the British Journal of Surgery published a randomized within-patient placebo-controlled trial of four single doses given at wound closure [7], and Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery reported a 60-patient trial after scar revision surgery [8].

Registered trials include phase II studies in split-skin graft donor sites, breast augmentation, breast reduction and varicose vein scars, and a 350-patient phase III trial in scar revision [14][16][17][15]. Wikipedia notes that phase III failed, with the developer's shares reported down about 75% on the 2011 news [12].

Because elevated TGF-beta3 appears in some late-stage tumours, a 2009 review examined its role in cancer, concluding functional data supporting a causative role are lacking and that some studies suggest a protective role [2].
Reviews list avotermin among emerging scar options alongside corticosteroids, lasers, silicone and others [4].
